n: The story of Esther takes place in Persia, among Jews who stayed in exile rather than returning to Judah. Ahasuerus is usually identified as Xerxes I, who ruled a vast empire from India to Ethiopia.

f.g: The Hebrew form of the Persian name Xšayaršā, known in Greek as Xerxes (reigned 486–465 BC), father of Artaxerxes I.
The Indus River region, in what is now Pakistan.
Hebrew Cush — the region south of Egypt (modern Sudan).

n: The king rules from Susa, one of Persia’s royal capitals, where Nehemiah later served as cupbearer.

f.g: The citadel of Susa, in what is now southwestern Iran.

n: In his third year (about 483 BC), the king throws a huge banquet for his officials and military leaders. Many think this gathering may have been connected to planning his war against Greece.

f.g: The two peoples that formed the core of the empire.

n: For six months the king shows off his wealth and splendor. The book often emphasizes royal excess — a world that seems all-powerful, yet God will quietly work behind it.

f.g: 180 days — about six months.

n: Then comes a seven-day banquet for everyone in the citadel, rich and poor, in the palace gardens.

f.g: Everyone, from the important to the ordinary.

n: The setting is dazzling: colored curtains, silver rings, marble columns, couches of gold and silver, and mosaic floors. Archaeologists have uncovered the palace at Susa, confirming its grandeur.

f.g: Couches for reclining at meals, as was the custom.
Curtains or awnings.

n: Drinks are served in gold cups, each one unique, with royal wine flowing freely.

f.g: Different from each other — no two alike.

f.w: according to the state of the king
f.g: With royal generosity.

n: Guests could drink as much or as little as they wished; no one was forced. The point is the king’s lavish freedom.

f.g: No one was required to drink a set amount.

n: Queen Vashti holds her own banquet for the women. Men and women sometimes feasted separately at royal events.

f.g: Possibly from a Persian word meaning “beautiful” or “best.”

n: On the last day, the king, drunk with wine, sends his seven personal attendants to bring the queen.

f.w: the heart of the king was merry with wine
f.g: He was drunk.
Eunuchs — trusted palace officials who served the royal household.

n: He wants to show off Vashti’s beauty to his drunken guests, wearing her royal crown. Many readers see this as a demeaning request.

f.g: The royal headdress worn by the queen.
Beautiful.

n: Vashti refuses. The text doesn’t say why, but her refusal to be displayed is often seen as an act of dignity. The king, used to total obedience, is furious.

f.g: Angry.

n: The king turns to his advisers, experts in law and custom, to decide what to do.

f.g: Wise men who understood precedents and customs (perhaps also astrologers).

n: These are the seven highest nobles, the inner circle with personal access to the king.

f.g: Who had direct personal access to the king — a rare privilege.

n: The all-powerful king asks what the law says to do with a queen who disobeyed. A personal embarrassment becomes a state matter.
Memucan argues that Vashti has wronged not just the king but every man in the empire. He turns a private refusal into a supposed threat to society.
He fears that wives everywhere will hear of it and look down on their husbands.

f.g: Treat their husbands with contempt.

n: The noblewomen will hear first and speak this way to their husbands. Memucan predicts endless contempt and conflict — a bit of humor at these powerful men’s insecurity.

f.g: Disrespect on the wives’ part and anger on the husbands’.

n: He proposes a royal decree, written into the unchangeable laws of the Persians and Medes, removing Vashti and giving her position to someone better. This sets the stage for Esther.

f.w: another that is better than she
f.g: Ironically fulfilled by Esther, through whom God saves His people.

n: Publishing the decree, he claims, will make all wives honor their husbands. Of course, true respect cannot be forced by law.

f.g: Respect.

n: The king and nobles like the idea and act on it.

f.g: The same phrase is used when Esther is chosen (Esther 2:4).

n: Letters are sent to every province in its own language, declaring that each man should rule his own household. The empire’s efficient postal system will play a major role later in the story.

f.w: to every people after their language
bear rule in his own house
f.g: Be master in his own home.
